proof_route: Convergence of the statistic and central sequence at parameter zero makes their joint laws tight. Extract one joint subsequence once at zero.

For each fixed local parameter, LAN transfers this same joint subsequence using bounded continuous tests and Gaussian exponential tilting. Finite-sample absolute continuity is not assumed: the singular alternative mass is bounded by the missing Radon-Nikodym mass, which tends to zero.
Control the exceptional zero-density event explicitly, since Lean defines Real.log 0 = 0. A metric approximation lemma transfers the LAN log expansion to the actual Radon-Nikodym density.

Disintegrate the joint base law and tilt only its Gaussian observation coordinate. The multivariate Gaussian exponential-density identity and the covariance map pull back the common kernel to the N(h,I inverse) input experiment.
assumption_comparison: Theorem 7.10 is stated for iid QMD experiments and Euclidean-valued statistics. The current Lean theorem starts directly from LAN and permits nonempty Polish Borel statistic spaces. The proof uses only LAN, tightness and standard-Borel disintegration, so those are legitimate extensions requiring explicit Lean adapters.
Theorem 9.3 assumes a dominated limit experiment; the nonsingular Gaussian shift satisfies this. The book omits its general proof, but gives the needed LAN special-case proof in Theorem 7.10.
No tightness assumption on T_n must be added: convergence under h=0 already supplies tightness in this target.

The conditional-kernel bridge requires a finite joint base measure, measurable nonnegative extended densities and a nonempty standard-Borel output space. The complete proof verifies these conditions from the original LAN hypotheses and also handles dimension zero.

citations.locator: Proposition 8.4, equivariant-in-law Gaussian estimator convolution; Bayesian proof

proof_route: The proved LAN representation theorem gives a single Gaussian randomization kernel for all local limits. Regularity makes the averaged output law a translate of L.

Gaussian location completeness identifies each translated input/output kernel with the original kernel Lebesgue-almost everywhere. Countable generation of the Borel sigma algebra promotes fixed-set equalities to equality of whole probability rows.

The residual kernel, which records output minus input, is translation invariant almost everywhere. A Haar-measure Fubini argument yields one almost-everywhere constant residual probability law M. This uses an existential constant, not an arbitrary representative such as the kernel at zero.
Absolute continuity transfers the residual identity to the Gaussian observation law. Kernel integration then gives L=N(0,I inverse) convolved with M.
assumption_comparison: The source QMD/iid assumptions are used to reach the representation theorem; the subsequent Gaussian equivariance proposition is a finite-sample Gaussian statement matching the needed LAN conclusion.
A finite covariance of L is not needed for convolution existence. It is needed only for the separate covariance-bound conclusion in the source, which is absent from the Lean theorem.
Do not impose pointwise equivariance on the kernel: regularity gives equivariance in law only.

Proposition 8.4 supplies a Bayesian proof of the Gaussian result. The local proof instead uses Gaussian completeness, proved from full natural exponential-family completeness, and an almost-everywhere translation-invariance argument. No prior-covariance limit or finite moment assumption on L is needed.
